questions.q: What is the first artifact this lesson recommends producing when designing a sharing model, before any configuration in Setup?
options: A sharing rule naming convention document
A list of every available Salesforce sharing feature
A finalized role hierarchy diagram
A requirements matrix mapping object x role/group to access level and business reason
questions.explain: The requirements matrix captures who needs what access and why before any mechanism is chosen, so the design can be checked for consistency before implementation.

questions.q: In the ordered design-decision sequence, what comes immediately after setting OWD per object?
options: Apex managed sharing
Manual sharing
Role hierarchy and territory hierarchy
Restriction rules
questions.explain: After OWD sets the floor, role and territory hierarchy establish the baseline grant that should do most of the structural work, before exceptions are layered on.

questions.q: A team sets every object's OWD to Public Read/Write specifically to avoid writing sharing rules, with no further review of who can see what. What failure mode does this describe?
options: Over-permissive sprawl
Over-restrictive rule pileup
Design ownership failure only
Account data skew
questions.explain: Setting OWD broad purely to dodge sharing-rule complexity, without deliberate justification, is over-permissive sprawl — it erodes real record-level control.

questions.q: Why is over-restrictive rule pileup also considered a design failure, rather than simply 'extra safe'?
options: Because Private OWD is against Salesforce's terms of service
Because it produces dozens of bespoke sharing rules per object that become unmaintainable and costly at scale
Because Private OWD disables the role hierarchy
Because it is impossible to combine Private OWD with sharing rules
questions.explain: Treating every access need as its own bespoke rule produces a pile of rules nobody can hold in their head and adds real performance and maintenance cost, which is its own kind of failure, not pure safety.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend to keep a sharing design correct as the business changes after launch?
options: Assigning ongoing ownership and a review cadence so rules stay mapped to current, valid business reasons
Rebuilding the entire sharing model from scratch every year regardless of actual drift
Freezing the design permanently once it passes initial review
Switching every object to Public Read/Write to eliminate the need for review
questions.explain: A sharing design needs an accountable owner and a periodic review cadence, mirroring the governance discipline used for data classification, or it degrades quietly over time.
